revealWordProblem.title: Apply: The 15 Puzzle
revealWordProblem.text:
The 15 Puzzle is a sliding puzzle with 15 numbered tiles in a frame 4 tiles high and 4 tiles wide. The goal is to arrange the tiles in order from 1 to 15 by sliding one tile at a time into the open space. Some starting arrangements can be solved and some cannot.
Question: Try solving the 15 Puzzle shown. Then make an argument for whether it is solvable or unsolvable.
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: A 4 by 4 sliding puzzle holding tiles numbered 1 to 15 with one empty space.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: I read the tiles in order, row by row, and counted how many pairs are out of order. A sideways slide never changes that count, and an up-or-down slide changes it in a way I can track along with the row the empty space is in. So I compared my starting count with what the finished puzzle needs, and used that comparison — not guessing and sliding — as the argument for whether this arrangement can reach 1 through 15 in order.

questions.stem: What is the fewest number of moves needed to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
questions.explanation: It takes at least 7 moves to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
choiceFeedback: 3 is the number of DISCS — moving each disc only once is impossible because of the size rule.
6 doubles the 3 discs but forgets the extra move — the pattern is double and add 1, so 3 discs need 7.
9 is 3 × 3, but the fewest-moves count follows the doubling pattern, not disc × disc.
hints: It is more than one move per disc.
A two-disc tower already takes 3 moves.
Double 3 and add 1.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el menor número de movimientos necesarios para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos?
questions.explanationEs: Se necesitan al menos 7 movimientos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos.
hintsEs: Es más de un movimiento por disco.
Una torre de dos discos ya toma 3 movimientos.
Duplica 3 y suma 1.

questions.stem: Which move is against the rules of the Tower of Hanoi?
choices: Placing a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Moving one disc at a time
Moving the top disc from a stack
Placing a smaller disc on top of a larger disc
questions.explanation: A larger disc can never be on top of a smaller disc — that is the rule that makes the puzzle a puzzle.
choiceFeedback: One disc at a time is exactly what the rules require, not what they forbid.
You may only move the TOP disc of a stack — that move follows the rules.
Smaller on top of larger is the legal direction; it is the reverse that is banned.
hints: Two of these are the rules themselves.
Think about disc SIZES.
Which stacking order would crush a smaller disc?
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál movimiento va contra las reglas de la Torre de Hanói?
questions.explanationEs: Un disco más grande nunca puede estar sobre uno más pequeño — esa es la regla que hace que el rompecabezas sea un rompecabezas.
hintsEs: Dos de estas son las reglas mismas.
Piensa en los TAMAÑOS de los discos.
¿Cuál orden de apilado aplastaría un disco más pequeño?

questions.stem: What will the solved puzzle look like?
choices: The discs in the same order — smallest on top to largest on bottom — but on a different rod
The discs in reverse order, largest on top
The discs spread out with one disc on each rod
The discs back on the starting rod in any order
questions.explanation: The goal is to rebuild the whole stack, smallest to largest, on a different rod.
choiceFeedback: Largest on top would break the rule — a larger disc can never sit on a smaller one.
Spreading the discs out is a middle step, not the finished puzzle.
The stack must END on a different rod, and the size order is required, not optional.
hints: Imagine the ending before you start.
The stack looks just like the start.
Only its rod has changed.
questions.explanationEs: La meta es reconstruir toda la pila, del más pequeño al más grande, en otra varilla.
hintsEs: Imagina el final antes de empezar.
La pila se ve igual que al inicio.
Solo cambió su varilla.

level1.stem: (Lesson 10.1) A planter is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide. What is its area?
level1.explanation: Area of a rectangle is length × width: 4 × 2 = 8 square feet.
choiceFeedback: 6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
12 comes from adding all four sides (4 + 2 + 4 + 2) — that is the perimeter, not the area.
2 comes from dividing 4 by 2 instead of multiplying.

The butterfly has exactly two wings
The butterfly's wings are very colorful
The butterfly is larger than most insects
level1.explanation: Symmetric means one side is a mirror image of the other — that is exactly what we see across the butterfly's body.
choiceFeedback: Having two wings is not enough — the two sides must MIRROR each other to be symmetric.
Color makes a butterfly pretty, but symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about color.
Size has nothing to do with symmetry — a tiny butterfly is just as symmetric as a big one.

level2.stem: The table shows 1 disc → 1 step, 2 discs → 3 steps, 3 discs → 7 steps. What is the pattern rule for the number of steps when you add one more disc?
choices: Double the number of steps and add 1
Add 2 to the number of steps
Add the number of discs to the steps
Multiply the number of steps by 3
level2.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so each new disc doubles the steps and adds 1.
choiceFeedback: Adding 2 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 + 2 = 5, and the table says 7.
Adding the discs fits 1 → 3 (1 + 2) but fails the next row: 3 + 3 = 6, and the table says 7.
Multiplying by 3 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 × 3 = 9, and the table says 7.
hints: Test each rule on BOTH jumps: 1 → 3 and 3 → 7.
Several rules pass the first jump; only one passes both.
What do you do to 3 to land exactly on 7?
level2.stemEs: La tabla muestra 1 disco → 1 paso, 2 discos → 3 pasos, 3 discos → 7 pasos. ¿Cuál es la regla del patrón para el número de pasos cuando agregas un disco más?

hintsEs: Prueba cada regla en LOS DOS saltos: 1 → 3 y 3 → 7.
Varias reglas pasan el primer salto; solo una pasa los dos.

level2.stem: Use the pattern rule to complete the table: how many steps for a four-disc tower?

9 adds 2 to 7 instead of doubling and adding 1.
28 multiplies 7 by 4 (the number of discs) instead of doubling once and adding 1.
hints: Start from the three-disc answer: 7 steps.

level2.stemEs: Usa la regla del patrón para completar la tabla: ¿cuántos pasos para una torre de cuatro discos?

hintsEs: Empieza con la respuesta de tres discos: 7 pasos.

level2.stem: What is the minimum number of steps to solve a FIVE-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
level2.explanation: A four-disc tower takes 15 steps, so a five-disc tower takes 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps.
choiceFeedback: 15 steps is the answer for FOUR discs — the fifth disc requires applying the rule once more.
30 doubles the 15 steps but forgets to add 1.
35 adds 5 discs × 4 to 15 — the rule is double and add 1, not add a multiple of the discs.
hints: You need the four-disc answer first: 15.
Apply the rule one more time.
level2.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el número mínimo de pasos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de CINCO discos?

hintsEs: Necesitas primero la respuesta de cuatro discos: 15.

choiceFeedback: The rules always apply — the pattern predicts the move COUNT, it does not change what moves are legal.

hints: What did the table tell us about the five-disc tower?

level2.stemEs: ¿Por qué encontrar un patrón es MÁS poderoso que solo resolver a mano el rompecabezas de tres discos?

level2.stem: Will the fewest number of steps for a Tower of Hanoi puzzle always be an ODD number?
choices: Yes — doubling any whole number gives an even number, and adding 1 makes it odd
No — every other tower size gives an even number of steps
Yes — but only because 7 happens to be odd
No — the steps alternate between odd and even
level2.explanation: Each answer comes from doubling the one before (always even) and adding 1 (always odd): 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 are all odd, and the rule guarantees the next one will be too.
choiceFeedback: Check the table: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — no even number ever appears.
It is not luck about 7 — the double-and-add-1 rule FORCES every result to be odd, forever.
The list 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 never alternates — every entry is odd.
hints: Look at the whole list: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.

How many days are in a year?
Multiply 8 × 365.
level2.stemEs: Una persona ahorra 8 galones de agua al día al abrir la llave solo para enjuagar. ¿Cuánta agua ahorra esa persona en un año (365 días)?
level2.explanationEs: 8 galones al día × 365 días = 2,920 galones en un año.
hintsEs: Conoces el ahorro por día.
¿Cuántos días tiene un año?
Multiplica 8 × 365.

level2.stem: (Lesson 10.1) If each person in a house saves 2,920 gallons a year, how much does a household of 3 people save in a year?
level2.explanation: 2,920 gallons per person × 3 people = 8,760 gallons a year.
choiceFeedback: 2,923 comes from adding 2,920 + 3 instead of multiplying.
973 (about 2,920 ÷ 3) divides instead of multiplying — more people save MORE water, not less.
5,840 multiplies by 2 people instead of 3.
hints: Each person saves the same amount.
3 people, each saving 2,920 gallons.
Multiply 2,920 × 3.
level2.stemEs: Si cada persona de una casa ahorra 2,920 galones al año, ¿cuánto ahorra en un año un hogar de 3 personas?
level2.explanationEs: 2,920 galones por persona × 3 personas = 8,760 galones al año.
hintsEs: Cada persona ahorra la misma cantidad.
3 personas, cada una ahorrando 2,920 galones.
Multiplica 2,920 × 3.

level2.stem: (Lesson 10.2) Why do people find symmetry pleasing?
choices: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance
Symmetric things are always brightly colored
Symmetry only appears in rare and expensive objects
Symmetric shapes are always larger than non-symmetric ones
level2.explanation: The lesson says it directly: our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.
choiceFeedback: Color is separate from symmetry — a plain gray moth can be perfectly symmetric.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature, from leaves to ladybugs — it is common, not rare.
Size has nothing to do with it — a tiny symmetric leaf is as balanced as a huge one.
hints: The answer is about how our brains respond.
What does bilateral symmetry provide that brains favor?
Think of an even, steady arrangement.
level2.stemEs: ¿Por qué a las personas les agrada la simetría?
level2.explanationEs: La lección lo dice directamente: nuestro cerebro está hecho para preferir el equilibrio, y la simetría bilateral da equilibrio.
hintsEs: La respuesta tiene que ver con cómo responde nuestro cerebro.
¿Qué proporciona la simetría bilateral que el cerebro prefiere?
Piensa en un arreglo parejo y constante.
choicesEs: Nuestro cerebro está hecho para preferir el equilibrio, y la simetría bilateral da equilibrio
Las cosas simétricas siempre tienen colores brillantes
La simetría solo aparece en objetos raros y caros
Las figuras simétricas siempre son más grandes que las no simétricas

level2.stem: (Lesson 10.2) There are over 17,000 species of butterflies, and ALL butterflies have reflective symmetry. About how many of those species have reflective symmetry?
choices: None — symmetry is only in plants
level2.explanation: 'All butterflies have reflective symmetry' means every one of the 17,000+ species — no exceptions.
choiceFeedback: 'All' means every single species, not half of them.
Symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about how colorful the wings are.
The butterfly itself was our first example — animals show bilateral symmetry too.
hints: Read the statement carefully: ALL butterflies.
Does 'all' leave any out?
Every species means every species.
level2.stemEs: Hay más de 17,000 especies de mariposas, y TODAS las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas de esas especies tienen simetría de reflexión?
level2.explanationEs: 'Todas las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión' significa cada una de las más de 17,000 especies — sin excepciones.
hintsEs: Lee el enunciado con cuidado: TODAS las mariposas.
¿'Todas' deja alguna fuera?
Cada especie significa cada especie.
choicesEs: Ninguna — la simetría solo está en las plantas

level2.stem: (Lesson 10.3) The table shows 1 disc → 1 step, 2 discs → 3 steps, 3 discs → 7 steps. What is the pattern rule for the number of steps when you add one more disc?
choices: Double the number of steps and add 1
Add 2 to the number of steps
Add the number of discs to the steps
Multiply the number of steps by 3
level2.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so each new disc doubles the steps and adds 1.
choiceFeedback: Adding 2 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 + 2 = 5, and the table says 7.
Adding the discs fits 1 → 3 (1 + 2) but fails the next row: 3 + 3 = 6, and the table says 7.
Multiplying by 3 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 × 3 = 9, and the table says 7.
hints: Test each rule on BOTH jumps: 1 → 3 and 3 → 7.
Several rules pass the first jump; only one passes both.
What do you do to 3 to land exactly on 7?
level2.stemEs: La tabla muestra 1 disco → 1 paso, 2 discos → 3 pasos, 3 discos → 7 pasos. ¿Cuál es la regla del patrón para el número de pasos cuando agregas un disco más?
level2.explanationEs: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 y 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, así que cada disco nuevo duplica los pasos y suma 1.
hintsEs: Prueba cada regla en LOS DOS saltos: 1 → 3 y 3 → 7.
Varias reglas pasan el primer salto; solo una pasa los dos.
¿Qué le haces al 3 para caer exactamente en 7?
choicesEs: Duplicar el número de pasos y sumar 1
Suma el número de discos a los pasos
Multiplicar el número de pasos por 3

level2.stem: (Lesson 10.3) Use the pattern rule to complete the table: how many steps for a four-disc tower?
level2.explanation: A three-disc tower takes 7 steps, so a four-disc tower takes 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps.
choiceFeedback: 14 doubles the 7 steps but forgets to add 1.
9 adds 2 to 7 instead of doubling and adding 1.
28 multiplies 7 by 4 (the number of discs) instead of doubling once and adding 1.
hints: Start from the three-disc answer: 7 steps.
Apply the rule: double, then add 1.
level2.stemEs: Usa la regla del patrón para completar la tabla: ¿cuántos pasos para una torre de cuatro discos?
level2.explanationEs: Una torre de tres discos toma 7 pasos, así que una torre de cuatro discos toma 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 pasos.
hintsEs: Empieza con la respuesta de tres discos: 7 pasos.
Aplica la regla: duplica y luego suma 1.

level3.stem: A five-disc tower takes 31 steps. Using the pattern rule, how many steps would a SIX-disc tower take?
level3.explanation: Apply the rule to 31: double it and add 1, so 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 steps.
choiceFeedback: 62 doubles the 31 steps but forgets to add 1.
36 adds 5 to 31 — the rule doubles the steps rather than adding the disc count.
32 adds 1 to 31 but forgets to double first.
hints: The rule works from any row of the table.
Double, then add 1.
level3.stemEs: Una torre de cinco discos toma 31 pasos. Usando la regla del patrón, ¿cuántos pasos tomaría una torre de SEIS discos?
level3.explanationEs: Aplica la regla a 31: duplícalo y suma 1, así que 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 pasos.
hintsEs: La regla funciona desde cualquier fila de la tabla.
Duplica y luego suma 1.

level3.stem: Look at the table a different way: 1 disc → 1, 2 discs → 3, 3 discs → 7, 4 discs → 15, 5 discs → 31. Which describes the relationship between the number of discs and the number of steps?
choices: The steps are 1 less than a doubling pattern: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 each minus 1
The steps are the number of discs multiplied by itself
The steps are 6 times the number of discs, plus or minus 1
The steps are the two previous step counts added together
level3.explanation: 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 8 − 1 = 7, 16 − 1 = 15, 32 − 1 = 31 — every entry is one less than the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
choiceFeedback: Discs times itself gives 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 — that misses the table from the second row on.
6 times the discs gives 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 — even allowing plus or minus 1, that fails the first rows.
Adding previous entries gives 1 + 3 = 4 for the third row, but the table says 7.
hints: Write the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 above the steps 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
Compare them row by row.
How far apart is each pair?
level3.stemEs: Mira la tabla de otra manera: 1 disco → 1, 2 discos → 3, 3 discos → 7, 4 discos → 15, 5 discos → 31. ¿Cuál describe la relación entre el número de discos y el número de pasos?
level3.explanationEs: 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 8 − 1 = 7, 16 − 1 = 15, 32 − 1 = 31 — cada valor es uno menos que el patrón que duplica 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
hintsEs: Escribe el patrón que duplica 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 arriba de los pasos 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
Compáralos fila por fila.
¿Qué tan separado está cada par?

level3.stem: The 15 Puzzle is a sliding puzzle with 15 tiles in a frame 4 tiles high by 4 tiles wide. You arrange the tiles from 1 to 15 by sliding one tile at a time into the open space. Sometimes it is solvable and sometimes it is not. How would you make an argument about whether a particular 15 Puzzle is solvable, using what this lesson taught about being playful?
level3.modelAnswer: I would play the way we played the Tower of Hanoi: start with small cases and look for patterns. The frame is 4 × 4 = 16 spaces holding 15 tiles, so there is exactly one open space to slide into. I would try to solve it, keep track of which arrangements I can reach, and look for a pattern or relationship in the tile positions that separates the solvable starting setups from the impossible ones. If every attempt at a certain arrangement fails the same way, that repeated pattern becomes my evidence for arguing it is unsolvable.
sentenceStems: My argument would use the pattern ___ .
level3.stemEs: El Rompecabezas del 15 es un rompecabezas deslizante con 15 fichas en un marco de 4 fichas de alto por 4 de ancho. Ordenas las fichas del 1 al 15 deslizando una a la vez hacia el espacio vacío. A veces tiene solución y a veces no. ¿Cómo construirías un argumento sobre si un Rompecabezas del 15 en particular tiene solución, usando lo que esta lección enseñó sobre ser juguetón?

level3.stem: The summary says playing with math lets us think differently by looking for patterns AND by imagining ways to visualize a problem. Describe how you used BOTH of those with the Tower of Hanoi.
level3.modelAnswer: I used imagination first: before moving anything, I pictured the solved puzzle — the same stack, smallest on top, standing on a different rod. Then I used patterns: I organized the small cases in a table (1 disc → 1 step, 2 → 3, 3 → 7) and found the double-and-add-1 rule, which predicted 15 steps for four discs and 31 for five. Imagining gave me the target, and the pattern gave me the count — together they solved towers I never touched.
sentenceStems: I found the pattern ___ , which predicted ___ .
level3.stemEs: El resumen dice que jugar con las matemáticas nos permite pensar de otra manera al buscar patrones Y al imaginar formas de visualizar un problema. Describe cómo usaste AMBAS con la Torre de Hanói.

level3.stem: Why is finding a pattern MORE powerful than just solving the three-disc puzzle by hand?
choices: The pattern predicts the answer for towers you have never played, like five or six discs
The pattern lets you skip the rules of the puzzle
Patterns make the discs move by themselves
A pattern proves the puzzle is impossible
level3.explanation: The pattern told us a five-disc tower needs a minimum of 31 steps — without moving a single disc.
choiceFeedback: The rules always apply — the pattern predicts the move COUNT, it does not change what moves are legal.
You still make every move yourself; the pattern only tells you how many to expect.
The pattern shows the puzzle IS solvable at every size, and says how many steps it takes.
hints: What did the table tell us about the five-disc tower?
Did we ever play the five-disc tower by hand?
Prediction is the power.
level3.stemEs: ¿Por qué encontrar un patrón es MÁS poderoso que solo resolver a mano el rompecabezas de tres discos?
level3.explanationEs: El patrón nos dijo que una torre de cinco discos necesita un mínimo de 31 pasos — sin mover ni un solo disco.
hintsEs: ¿Qué nos dijo la tabla sobre la torre de cinco discos?
¿Alguna vez jugamos a mano la torre de cinco discos?
Predecir es lo poderoso.
choicesEs: El patrón predice la respuesta para torres que nunca has jugado, como de cinco o seis discos
El patrón te deja saltarte las reglas del rompecabezas
Los patrones hacen que los discos se muevan solos
Un patrón demuestra que el rompecabezas es imposible

level3.stem: Before solving, the lesson asked you to DESCRIBE what the solution will look like. Why is imagining the ending a useful way to start a puzzle?
level3.modelAnswer: Imagining the ending gives me a target. Once I know the discs must end up smallest-on-top on a different rod, I can judge every move by whether it gets me closer to that picture. Math can help us imagine what might happen before it happens.
sentenceStems: Then each move can be judged by ___ .
level3.stemEs: Antes de resolver, la lección te pidió DESCRIBIR cómo se verá la solución. ¿Por qué imaginar el final es una manera útil de empezar un rompecabezas?
sentenceStemsEs: Entonces cada movimiento se puede juzgar según ___ .

level3.stem: Will the fewest number of steps for a Tower of Hanoi puzzle always be an ODD number?
choices: Yes — doubling any whole number gives an even number, and adding 1 makes it odd
No — every other tower size gives an even number of steps
Yes — but only because 7 happens to be odd
No — the steps alternate between odd and even
level3.explanation: Each answer doubles the one before it, which is always even. Then you add 1, which makes it odd. Check the list: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 are all odd. The rule guarantees the next one will be odd too.
choiceFeedback: Check the table: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — no even number ever appears.
It is not luck about 7 — the double-and-add-1 rule FORCES every result to be odd, forever.
The list 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 never alternates — every entry is odd.
hints: Look at the whole list: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
What kind of number is 'double anything'?
What happens when you add 1 to an even number?
level3.stemEs: ¿El menor número de pasos de la Torre de Hanói siempre será un número IMPAR?
level3.explanationEs: Cada respuesta duplica la anterior, lo que siempre da un número par. Después sumas 1, lo que lo hace impar. Revisa la lista: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 son todos impares. La regla garantiza que el siguiente también será impar.
hintsEs: Mira toda la lista: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
¿Qué tipo de número es 'el doble de cualquier cosa'?
¿Qué pasa cuando le sumas 1 a un número par?
choicesEs: Sí — duplicar cualquier número entero da un número par, y sumarle 1 lo hace impar
No — todos los demás tamaños de torre dan un número par de pasos
Sí — pero solo porque 7 resulta ser impar
No — los pasos alternan entre impares y pares

level3.stem: (Lesson 10.1) Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year. Which correctly compares households of 3, 4, 5, and 8 people?
level3.explanation: Multiply 2,920 by each household size. For 3 people: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. For 4 and 5 people: 11,680 and 14,600. For 8 people: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
choiceFeedback: 20,440 is 7 × 2,920 — the last household has 8 people, not 7.
Those add the household size to 2,920 instead of multiplying by it.
46,720 is 16 × 2,920 — that doubles the 8-person household instead of computing it.
hints: Each household total is people × 2,920.
Check the last value most carefully.
level3.stemEs: Cada persona ahorra 2,920 galones al año. ¿Cuál compara correctamente hogares de 3, 4, 5 y 8 personas?
level3.explanationEs: Multiplica 2,920 por cada tamaño de hogar. Para 3 personas: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. Para 4 y 5 personas: 11,680 y 14,600. Para 8 personas: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
hintsEs: El total de cada hogar es personas × 2,920.
Revisa el último valor con más cuidado.

level3.stem: (Lesson 10.2) Your friend insists that only ONE of two flowers has bilateral symmetry, but both pass the mirror-image test — just across lines pointing in different directions. What is the best response?
choices: Both flowers have bilateral symmetry — a line of symmetry does not have to point the same direction in every figure
Your friend is right, because a real line of symmetry must always be vertical
Neither flower has bilateral symmetry, because flowers are not animals
Agree with your friend, because two people should not disagree about math
level3.explanation: The test for bilateral symmetry is whether SOME line makes the two sides mirror images — the direction of that line does not matter.
choiceFeedback: Nothing in the definition requires vertical — a mirror line can run in any direction.
Plants have bilateral symmetry too; the leaf layers in this very lesson were the example.
Math disagreements are settled with evidence and a test, not with politeness.
hints: Apply the same test to both flowers.
Does the definition say which direction the line must point?
If a mirror line exists, the symmetry exists.
level3.stemEs: Tu amigo insiste en que solo UNA de dos flores tiene simetría bilateral, pero ambas pasan la prueba de la imagen reflejada — solo que con líneas que apuntan en direcciones distintas. ¿Cuál es la mejor respuesta?
level3.explanationEs: La prueba de la simetría bilateral es si ALGUNA línea hace que los dos lados sean imágenes reflejadas — la dirección de esa línea no importa.
hintsEs: Aplica la misma prueba a las dos flores.
¿La definición dice en qué dirección debe apuntar la línea?
Si existe un eje de reflexión, existe la simetría.
choicesEs: Ambas flores tienen simetría bilateral — un eje de simetría no tiene que apuntar en la misma dirección en cada figura
Tu amigo tiene razón, porque un eje de simetría verdadero siempre debe ser vertical
Ninguna flor tiene simetría bilateral, porque las flores no son animales
Estar de acuerdo con tu amigo, porque dos personas no deberían estar en desacuerdo sobre matemáticas

level3.stem: (Lesson 10.3) A five-disc tower takes 31 steps. Using the pattern rule, how many steps would a SIX-disc tower take?
level3.explanation: Apply the rule to 31: double it and add 1, so 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 steps.
choiceFeedback: 62 doubles the 31 steps but forgets to add 1.
36 adds 5 to 31 — the rule doubles the steps rather than adding the disc count.
32 adds 1 to 31 but forgets to double first.
hints: The rule works from any row of the table.
Double, then add 1.
level3.stemEs: Una torre de cinco discos toma 31 pasos. Usando la regla del patrón, ¿cuántos pasos tomaría una torre de SEIS discos?
level3.explanationEs: Aplica la regla a 31: duplícalo y suma 1, así que 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 pasos.
hintsEs: La regla funciona desde cualquier fila de la tabla.
Duplica y luego suma 1.

tool.title: Fewest Moves in Tower of Hanoi
tool.caption: Each bar doubles the one before it and adds 1: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. One more disc nearly doubles the work, so the bars grow far faster than the disc count.
